questions.prompt: A research engineer on an interpretability team spends a week stuck on why a distributed training run silently diverges at 64 GPUs but not at 8, while a teammate carrying the title "Research Scientist" spends that same week stuck on whether the underlying idea is even right. Per Lesson 1, what does this contrast actually illustrate?
options: The research engineer and research scientist roles have a hard boundary that keeps each from doing the other's work
This is a difference in "center of gravity" between the two roles — a spectrum of emphasis in what tends to get stuck, not a strict division of labor
The research engineer is doing lower-value work than the research scientist on this team
Labs like Anthropic and OpenAI never post Research Engineer roles on the same team as Research Scientist roles
questions.explain: Lesson 1 is explicit that the two titles describe a center of gravity, not a fence: 'what being stuck looks like' is one of the listed divergence points, with the research engineer's version (a distributed run diverging only at scale) and the research scientist's version (whether the idea is right) given as the exact illustrative contrast. The lesson also notes major labs post both titles on the same team with overlapping work, which rules out a hard boundary.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: practices that protect a result's statistical validity — correct seeding, apples-to-apples comparisons, catching a silent NaN before it gets averaged into a metric — are collectively called ________, per Lesson 2.
questions.explain: Lesson 2 names experiment hygiene as the specific set of practices research engineering spends its risk-management effort on, in contrast to product engineering's focus on edge cases and backward compatibility.

questions.prompt: Select every item below that Lesson 2 identifies as a product-engineering instinct that actively MISLEADS a new research engineer, as opposed to a skill that transfers directly.
options: Handle every edge case, even ones your current experiment can't hit
Abstract early for reuse, since research code changes shape weekly
Code review gates every merge, with no distinction between a one-off notebook and a change to the shared training library
Version control discipline, even if branching conventions get looser
Debugging methodology: bisecting, isolating variables, reading stack traces
questions.explain: Lesson 2 lists 'handle every edge case,' 'abstract early for reuse,' and 'code review gates every merge' as the three instincts that actively mislead in a research context, because they spend effort research teams can't afford on inputs, reuse, and process rigor the work doesn't need yet. Version control discipline and debugging methodology are listed in the same lesson as skills that transfer directly from product engineering, unchanged.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of a research engineer's typical daily rhythm, per Lesson 3, in the order they tend to occur.
items: Triage: check overnight runs, dashboards, and alerts to decide what needs attention first
Build or fix: write a new data-loading path, fix a flagged bug, or implement a technique from a paper the team wants to try
Launch and wait: kick off a run or sweep, then shift to other work while it executes
Check in on long runs: look back periodically at jobs still going, catching problems early rather than only at the end
Discuss and write up: share a result in a team channel or short note, explaining what changed and what it means next
questions.explain: Lesson 3 describes this exact rough order — triage, build or fix, launch and wait, check in on long runs, discuss and write up — while noting the day is frequently interrupted and revisited rather than followed as a rigid schedule, since the day is paced by compute cycles, not the clock.

questions.prompt: A researcher reproduces a paper's result using the authors' own code, matched hyperparameters, and multiple seeds, but only has enough compute to train at one-tenth the original scale and for a fraction of the original training steps. The direction and rough shape of the result holds — the proposed method still beats the baseline — but the absolute numbers differ substantially from the paper's reported values. Which reproduction tier, per Lesson 7, does this result correctly support claiming?
options: Qualitative trend match — the direction and rough shape of the result holds even though the absolute numbers differ, often because of a smaller compute budget
Exact match within noise — the number falls within the variance expected from re-running with different seeds
Match within a reasonable tolerance — close enough that the practical conclusion doesn't change even if exact digits differ
A failed reproduction, since the absolute numbers don't match the published value
A full reproduction of the paper's exact claim, since the direction of the effect matches
None of the three tiers apply when compute is scaled down — scaled-down results can't be classified at all
questions.explain: Lesson 7 defines three reproduction tiers of decreasing strength: exact match within noise, match within tolerance, and qualitative trend match. A result obtained at one-tenth the scale and a fraction of the training steps, where only the direction and rough shape of the effect hold while the absolute numbers differ substantially, is exactly what a qualitative trend match describes — a real but weaker claim than the other two tiers, and the honest move is to label it as such rather than imply more.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C (match within tolerance) sounds close, but that tier means the scaled-down number is close enough in absolute terms that the practical conclusion wouldn't change — it still requires landing near the reported value, not just pointing in the same direction. A run at one-tenth scale with substantially different absolute numbers hasn't earned tolerance match; it has earned the weaker qualitative trend match, and conflating the two is exactly the kind of quietly-upgraded claim Lesson 7 warns against.

questions.prompt: A paper claims its new gating mechanism improves performance. Its ablation table removes the gating mechanism but also switches to a different learning-rate schedule in that same ablated run. Per Lesson 6, what's the problem with this ablation?
options: Nothing — ablations are allowed to change multiple things as long as the headline comparison is reported
The ablation no longer isolates the gating mechanism's effect — it measures the combined effect of two changes, which is a different and weaker claim
The ablation should have removed the gating mechanism and the learning-rate schedule change at the same time to be thorough
The ablation is invalid because it didn't also change the baseline's batch size
questions.explain: Lesson 6 warns specifically about an ablation that removes a component but also changes something else incidentally, like a learning-rate schedule — the ablation then no longer isolates what the claim is about, and the result measures the combined effect of whatever changed rather than giving direct evidence about the gating mechanism alone.

questions.prompt: A team reports a new method beating a baseline that was copied verbatim, unmodified, from a three-year-old paper and trained for the same relatively small number of steps the baseline always used. Select every reproducibility pitfall from Lesson 8 that this scenario could plausibly involve.
options: Baseline tuning gap — the comparison baseline may not have received tuning effort comparable to the new method
Dataset drift — the exact dataset version may have changed since the three-year-old baseline paper was published
Hyperparameter sweep leakage — the new method's hyperparameters may have been selected via a validation-set sweep the baseline never got the same chance at
Compute-dependent results — the comparison is only questionable if it ran on completely different hardware with a different batch size, which this scenario doesn't mention
This is almost certainly deliberate fraud, since the baseline is three years old
questions.explain: Lesson 8 names an unmodified, stale baseline run for a fixed number of steps as a classic sign of a baseline tuning gap, and notes that datasets get revised or rebalanced over time, making a three-year-old baseline's exact data version worth checking. It also flags undisclosed hyperparameter sweeps on the new method as a separate, compounding issue. The lesson is explicit that most reproduction failures aren't deliberate misconduct, and nothing in this scenario involves a hardware or batch-size difference.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: before contacting a paper's authors about a failed reproduction, Lesson 9 says you should first rule out ________ — changes in library, CUDA, or Python versions between when the paper was released and when you're running it, since this is one of the most common silent causes of a mismatch.
questions.explain: Lesson 9 names dependency drift specifically, as part of ruling out your own setup before escalating to issue trackers or the authors themselves.

questions.prompt: Match each paper-reading term from Lesson 5 to what it actually describes.
right: Reading title, abstract, headings, conclusion, and figures first to decide whether a paper merits more time
The distance between how strongly a sentence is worded and how strongly the actual data backs it up
Closely reading the method and limitations sections before the full results, then related work, appendix, and code
Keshav's method of a cheap skim, a structural read, and a deep reconstruction, done in that order and only as far as each pass justifies
questions.explain: The three-pass approach is Keshav's overall method of a cheap skim, a structural read, and a deep reconstruction. The skimming pass is the cheap first step (title, abstract, headings, conclusion, figures). The deep pass reads method and limitations before results, then related work, appendix, and code. The claim-evidence gap is the distance between a claim's wording and the strength of its actual supporting data.

questions.prompt: A critical data-loading function exists only inside a notebook cell. Six months later, nobody on the team can find it to reproduce a result that depended on it. Per Lesson 11, what does this illustrate, and what's the fix?
options: Nothing is wrong — notebooks are the correct home for any code that's actually used
This is a problem with git, not repo layout — the function should have been committed more often

This is the single most common failure mode in research repos, exactly the kind the src/ vs. scripts/ vs. notebooks/ separation is meant to prevent — the function should have lived in src/ since the result depended on it
Notebooks are inherently unreproducible and should never be used anywhere in a research codebase
questions.explain: Lesson 11's organizing principle is that anything another file imports from — or that a result depends on — lives in src/; anything you just run lives in scripts/, and notebooks are for exploration only. A load-bearing data-loading function buried in a notebook cell, unfindable later, is explicitly called out as the single most common failure mode this layout is designed to prevent.

questions.prompt: Select every item below that Lesson 13 identifies as technical debt that's genuinely FINE to carry in research code.
options: No input validation on an internal-only function you're the only caller of
Hard-coded paths and magic numbers during exploration
Duplicated code across two experiment variants instead of a premature shared abstraction
Comprehensive error handling for inputs that actually can occur in your current, controlled experiment
Zero test coverage on the shared training loop that every experiment on the team imports
questions.explain: Lesson 13 lists no input validation on internal-only functions, hard-coded paths/magic numbers during exploration, and duplicated code across variants as debt that's genuinely fine in research code. It explicitly reverses the fourth option — the debt that's fine is skipping handling for inputs that CAN'T occur, not ones that can — and it calls out shared infrastructure like the training loop as exactly the part of the codebase that still needs production-grade testing because many experiments depend on it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: training a model on one fixed batch for many steps and asserting the loss drops sharply is called the ________ test, and Lesson 14 calls it the single highest-value correctness check in ML code.
questions.explain: Lesson 14 names the overfit-a-batch test as the highest-value test in ML code, because a model that can't drive the loss down on one batch it's allowed to memorize reveals a fundamental wiring problem before a day of compute gets wasted on a full run.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order Lesson 16 describes for making sure a launched run's provenance is fully recoverable later.
items: Check the working tree for uncommitted changes before launching, and commit or stash if any exist
Read the current commit hash with git rev-parse HEAD
Log the commit hash as a field in the experiment-tracking run's config, alongside the resolved Hydra config
Optionally tag the commit (e.g. git tag paper-table2-row3) if the run turns out to produce a headline result
questions.explain: Lesson 16 guards against the dirty-working-tree trap first, since a commit hash is worthless if uncommitted changes were actually what ran. Only then does reading and logging the commit hash alongside the resolved config make the run's provenance recoverable, with tagging a headline-result commit as a final, optional lightweight habit.

questions.prompt: Match each code-review term from Lesson 15 to what it actually means.
right: Approving the sound majority of a diff while flagging a smaller concern as a fast follow-up, instead of stalling the whole PR
A change to a configuration file, such as a Hydra YAML, that can silently change experiment behavior just as much as a code change can
How much of the codebase or how many experiments a given change could affect; review intensity should scale with it
Correctness and experiment-validity concerns block a merge; style preferences are offered only as optional comments
questions.explain: A config diff is a configuration-file change that can be as consequential as code. Blast radius is how much of the codebase or how many experiments a change could affect. Blocking vs. non-blocking feedback separates correctness concerns (block) from style preferences (don't block). Partial unblocking is approving the sound majority of a diff while flagging a smaller concern as a follow-up.

questions.prompt: A team has a fixed budget of 40 training runs on 4 GPUs to tune 3 hyperparameters, where individual training runs take several hours each and only limited parallelism is available. Which search strategy does Lesson 18 recommend as the best fit for this specific situation, and why?
options: Bayesian search, because its sample efficiency matters most when individual trials are expensive and parallelism is limited, even though it's inherently sequential
Grid search, because it guarantees exhaustive coverage of the 3-parameter space regardless of budget
Random search, because it always outperforms Bayesian search when only a few hyperparameters matter
Grid search, because it parallelizes better than Bayesian search across exactly 4 GPUs
Random search, because Bayesian search cannot be used when a budget is fixed in advance
Whichever method requires the fewest configuration files to set up, since that's the only real constraint on a 40-run budget
questions.explain: Lesson 18's rule of thumb is to use Bayesian search specifically when individual runs are expensive (hours or days) and parallelism is limited — exactly this situation — because its sample efficiency more than makes up for being inherently sequential. Grid search over even a modest 3-parameter space scales badly and gives no way to spend a limited budget where it's most informative, and random search, while a strong default with many parallel workers, doesn't match Bayesian search's sample efficiency when trials are this costly.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C correctly states that random search often outperforms grid search for a fixed budget when only a few hyperparameters matter — that's Bergstra and Bengio's actual result cited in Lesson 18. But that's a comparison against grid search specifically, not a claim that random search beats Bayesian search in general. Lesson 18's rule of thumb is the opposite for this exact situation: when trials are expensive and parallelism is limited, Bayesian search's sample efficiency wins out over random search's broader but less targeted exploration.

questions.prompt: A sweep samples learning rate uniformly (linearly) between 1e-5 and 1e-2. Per Lesson 17, what's wrong with this choice?
options: Nothing is wrong, linear sampling is always appropriate for any numeric hyperparameter

Learning rate's effect is roughly multiplicative, not additive, so a linear-uniform sample wastes the overwhelming majority of samples above 1e-3, where dynamics are already unstable for most architectures — a log-uniform distribution is the right fit instead
The range itself is wrong; learning rate should always be swept between 0 and 1 on a linear scale
Linear sampling is fine for learning rate but would be wrong for dropout, which needs a log scale instead
questions.explain: Lesson 17 explains that learning rate and weight decay are swept on a log scale because their effect on training is roughly multiplicative, and a linear-uniform sample over a wide range like 1e-5 to 1e-2 wastes most of its samples above 1e-3, where the dynamics are already unstable for most architectures. Dropout is the opposite case — it lives in a narrow, roughly linear range, so a plain uniform distribution is the correct choice there.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about ablation study design, per Lesson 22.
options: Each row of an ablation table should correspond to exactly one change from the full model, not a bundle of changes
If an ablated variant trains for fewer steps because it converges 'faster,' comparing it against the baseline anyway is fine as long as both reach their own natural stopping point
A single run per variant is sufficient as long as the difference looks large on inspection
Removing a component that produces a degenerate, untrainable model calls for a controlled substitute variant instead of a literal ablation
The baseline for testing whether a specific internal component matters should be the full model with that component removed, compared under identical conditions to the full model with it present
questions.explain: Lesson 22 requires exactly one change per ablation row, and defines the correct baseline for an internal-component claim as the full model with that component removed vs. present, under identical conditions. It also covers the degenerate-ablation case explicitly: a component so load-bearing that removing it breaks training needs a substitute variant instead. The lesson explicitly rejects different training budgets across variants as a confound (not something to wave through) and explicitly requires repeated seeds with reported variance, not a single run.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in experiment-tracking infrastructure, large binary files like model checkpoints should be logged to a separate ________ rather than attached to every metric-logging call, so the metrics database stays fast to query, per Lesson 19.
questions.explain: Lesson 19 treats checkpoints and datasets as a separate, blob-oriented concern from metric logging, backed by its own artifact store (W&B Artifacts, MLflow's artifact store) so the metrics database doesn't get bloated with multi-gigabyte files.

questions.prompt: Match each compute-scheduling term from Lesson 20 to what it actually controls.
right: Jobs tagged with a priority level jump the queue ahead of lower-priority ones
A hard per-user or per-team cap on concurrent resource usage, enforced independently of priority scoring
Suspending or killing a lower-priority running job to free resources for a higher-priority one, then automatically requeuing it
The scheduler tracks each user's recent resource usage and lowers their effective priority the more they've already consumed
questions.explain: Priority lets a tagged job jump the queue. Fair-share lowers a heavy user's effective priority based on recent consumption. Preemption suspends or kills a lower-priority job to free resources, then requeues it. A quota is a hard per-user or per-team cap, enforced independently of priority scoring.

questions.prompt: What does this Slurm job array submission actually do, per Lesson 24?
options: Submits a single job that runs 40 times sequentially inside one allocation, sharing one log file

Submits 40 indexed copies of the same job script as one Slurm submission, each with its own $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID value used here to select a different config file, and (per the %A/%a output path tokens) its own log file
Submits exactly one job that requests 40 GPUs simultaneously
Fails, because Slurm job arrays can't be combined with per-trial config files
questions.explain: Lesson 24 describes a job array as a single submission that runs many indexed copies of the same job script, each getting its own $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID at runtime, used here to pick a different config file per trial. The %A/%a output path tokens route each array element's log to its own file automatically, so trials run as separate scheduled jobs, not sequentially inside one allocation.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about DVC (Data Version Control), per Lesson 26.
options: DVC tracks a lightweight pointer file (.dvc) in git while the actual data lives in a separate remote like S3 or GCS
DVC identifies data by a hash of its content, so two files with the same content get the same hash regardless of filename
Checking out an old git commit and running dvc pull fetches the exact data version that commit's .dvc pointer refers to
DVC stores the actual dataset bytes directly inside git's object store, the same way git stores code
Content-addressed storage means file modification dates are the authoritative way to check if two datasets are the same version
questions.explain: Lesson 26 describes DVC as tracking a small .dvc pointer in git while the real data sits in a remote, identified by a content hash so identical content always hashes the same regardless of filename. Checking out an old commit and running dvc pull recovers the exact matching data version. The lesson explicitly contrasts this with plain git, which would have to store every historical version of the data itself — exactly what DVC avoids — and it explicitly says to compare hashes rather than modification dates or file sizes, which can lie.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 23, a Slurm job that has been submitted but is still waiting for its requested resources to free up is in the ________ state.
questions.explain: Lesson 23 lists pending, running, and a terminal state (completed, failed, timeout, or cancelled) as the states a job moves through, with pending meaning it's waiting for resources and its queue position set by the scheduling policy.

questions.prompt: A trial inside a Slurm sweep failed and is no longer in the live queue. Put these diagnostic steps in the order Lesson 24 describes for tracking down what happened.
items: Check squeue -u $USER and notice the job is no longer listed in the live queue
Run sacct -u $USER --format=JobID,JobName,State,Elapsed,ExitCode to pull historical job records
Identify the failed trial's exit code and job ID from the sacct output
Open that trial's log file at the path given by the job's %A/%a output tokens to see the actual error
questions.explain: Lesson 24 draws a direct contrast between squeue (only active/pending jobs) and sacct (completed job history with exit codes), naming sacct as the first place to check why a sweep job failed once it's no longer in the live queue, before tracking down the specific trial's own log file via the %A/%a-tokenized output path.

questions.code:
scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler()

with torch.cuda.amp.autocast():
    loss = compute_loss(model, batch)

scaler.scale(loss).backward()
scaler.unscale_(optimizer)
torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
scaler.step(optimizer)
scaler.update()
questions.prompt: A team trains a transformer in fp16 mixed precision using torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler, applying gradient clipping via clip_grad_norm_ after calling scaler.unscale_(optimizer). Which statement correctly describes what each piece is actually doing, per Lesson 29?
options: Loss scaling pushes small gradients up into fp16's representable range before backward to avoid silent underflow, scaler.unscale_ restores their true magnitude before clipping, and gradient clipping then caps the gradient norm independently of precision to prevent a single unstable batch from corrupting the weights
Loss scaling and gradient clipping are two names for the same operation, both of which only matter in fp32 training
Gradient clipping is what prevents fp16 underflow; loss scaling is only used to speed up training, not for numerical correctness
scaler.unscale_ must be called after the optimizer step, not before, or the clipping will be computed on the wrong values
bf16 requires the exact same loss-scaling machinery as fp16, since both have the same exponent range
GradScaler's job is to convert fp32 weights permanently into fp16 weights before training begins
questions.explain: Lesson 29 lays out exactly this pipeline: loss scaling multiplies the loss before backward so small gradients don't silently underflow to zero in fp16's narrow exponent range; scaler.unscale_ then restores gradients to their true magnitude before anything inspects or modifies them; gradient clipping is a separate, precision-independent safety net that caps the gradient norm to prevent one unstable batch from corrupting the weights. The two mechanisms solve different problems and are applied in that specific order for a reason.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D gets the order backwards. The required sequence from Lesson 29 is scale -> backward -> unscale -> clip -> step: unscale_ has to run before clipping (so the clip threshold applies to true-magnitude gradients) and before the optimizer step (so the optimizer applies real, not scaled-up, gradients). Calling unscale_ after the step, as this option suggests, would mean the optimizer already updated weights using artificially inflated gradients — exactly backwards from what the code shown actually does.

questions.code:
preds = model(x)          # shape (B,)
targets = y                # shape (B, 1)  -- an unintentional extra dim

loss = ((preds - targets) ** 2).mean()
questions.prompt: What actually happens when this code runs, and why is it dangerous per Lesson 28?
options: preds (B,) broadcasts against targets (B,1) to produce a (B,B) intermediate instead of the intended elementwise (B,) comparison — the code runs without error and produces a plausible but wrong loss value
PyTorch raises a shape-mismatch error immediately, so the bug can never reach a reported result
The subtraction automatically reshapes targets to (B,), making the result correct
This only matters if B is larger than 1,000
questions.explain: Lesson 28 names this exact pattern — broadcasting instead of elementwise comparison — as the single most common silent bug in a research codebase. The mismatched shapes broadcast to produce a (B,B) result instead of the intended (B,), the .mean() call still runs and still produces a number, and that number is simply wrong, with no exception raised to catch it.

questions.prompt: A researcher runs the sanity checks from Lesson 31 on a new architecture. Select every statement below that correctly describes what one of these checks actually tells you.
options: If overfitting a single batch plateaus well above zero loss, something in the model, loss, or optimizer wiring is broken
A parameter with requires_grad=True but p.grad is None after backward() is a sign it's detached from the computation graph or never touched by the forward pass
If replacing real input with random noise barely changes the loss, the model is probably using the input correctly and efficiently
A sophisticated model scoring worse than a trivial predict-the-mean baseline is a sign something is wrong, not just a sign the architecture needs more tuning
These four checks, run once when a codebase is new, don't need to be repeated for later experiments built on top of it
questions.explain: Lesson 31 states that a batch that won't overfit to near-zero indicates broken wiring, a parameter with no gradient is likely detached or unused, and a model scoring at or below a trivial baseline hasn't learned anything meaningful yet. The input-ablation check is inverted in option C: the lesson says if noise barely changes the loss, the model ISN'T actually using the input the way you think. The lesson also explicitly says to run this checklist at the start of every new experimental direction, not just once on a new codebase.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: to verify a custom autograd.Function's manual backward pass without knowing the "right" output in advance, Lesson 30 recommends torch.autograd.________, which numerically estimates a gradient via finite differences and compares it to the analytical gradient.
questions.explain: Lesson 30 names gradcheck as the standard way to verify a custom backward pass independent of any task-level metric, since it only checks internal consistency between forward and backward, not whether the output is 'correct' in any absolute sense.

questions.prompt: A tracked metric has plateaued with no crashes and no NaNs, and Lesson 31's sanity checks all pass. Put these diagnostic steps in the cost-ordered sequence Lesson 32 recommends.
items: Run a short learning-rate sweep across orders of magnitude on a small subset of data
Plot the training loss and the tracked metric on the same x-axis to check they're actually correlated
Check the label distribution and deduplication of the dataset for a collapse
Substantially increase model size on a small subset to see whether the plateau moves, if everything else has checked out
questions.explain: Lesson 32 orders the checks by cost: a learning-rate sweep takes minutes, so it's ruled out first; a loss/metric correlation check is cheap and catches a mismatch between what's optimized and what's watched; a label-distribution check takes seconds and catches a data problem wearing a training-problem costume; only after all of that is capacity (increasing model size) worth investigating, since redesigning an architecture is the most expensive hypothesis to test.

questions.prompt: A research report is organized as: 'First I tried X, which didn't work. Then I tried Y, which also had issues. Then Z finally worked.' Per Lesson 33, what's the problem with this structure?
options: Nothing — chronological order is always the clearest way to present a research finding
It forces the reader to reconstruct the actual finding from a narrative, burying what the reader most needs: the claim, stated plainly, up front
The report should instead only ever describe Z and omit X and Y entirely
This structure is fine as long as the report is under one page
questions.explain: Lesson 33 calls this exact chronological structure the most common structural mistake in a research report, because it buries the one thing the reader most needs — what you actually believe now, and how strongly — behind a narrative they have to reconstruct themselves. The fix is leading with the claim, then using the rest of the document, including what didn't work, to establish and qualify it.

questions.prompt: Before reporting an experiment as a genuine negative result, select every 'mundane explanation' Lesson 34 says should be ruled out first.
options: Whether the new approach's learning rate was swept independently, since a method that needs a different LR than the baseline will look broken if evaluated at the baseline's LR
Whether the baseline was actually run with the same data and compute budget as the treatment
Whether the sanity checks from the debugging chapter (overfitting a tiny batch, gradients reaching every parameter) actually passed for the new code path
Whether the result would make an interesting conference talk
Whether enough seeds were run to distinguish a real null effect from noise
questions.explain: Lesson 34 lists checking the baseline's data and budget parity, sweeping the new method's LR independently, confirming the debugging chapter's sanity checks pass for the new code path, and running enough seeds to distinguish a real effect from noise — all as mundane, checkable explanations to rule out before a negative result is reported as a genuine finding rather than a disguised bug report. Whether a result would make an interesting talk has nothing to do with this technical ruling-out process.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 35 recommends tracking research progress as falsifiable ________ — each paired with the specific experiment that would show it's false and the compute budget allocated to testing it — rather than as a list of tasks.
questions.explain: Lesson 35 proposes hypothesis tracking as a more honest unit of research progress than a task-based sprint board, since a research question's effort isn't knowable in advance the way a software ticket's is.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lesson 36 to what it actually describes.
right: An uncontrolled difference between a treatment and baseline that makes the comparison's result ambiguous or uninterpretable
The specific value an engineer adds by making many experiment variants cheap and reproducible to run, rather than writing the research idea itself
Translating a conceptually simple ask into an explicit trade-off between a rough version available immediately and a rigorous version that takes longer
Filling in the unspecified details — controls, confounds, held-fixed variables — of a scientist's question so it becomes a well-defined, defensible experiment
questions.explain: Scoping a 'quick' request means making explicit the trade-off between a rough version now and a rigorous version later. Experiment design translation means filling in the unspecified controls and confounds of a scientist's question. A confound is an uncontrolled difference that makes a comparison ambiguous. Infrastructure leverage is the value an engineer adds by making many variants cheap to run.

questions.prompt: A reviewer writes: 'I think the sparsity idea probably does help here, but one seed with no learning-rate sweep for the sparse variant doesn't show that yet.' Per Lesson 37, what does this feedback correctly do?
options: It rejects the underlying hypothesis as implausible
It separates feedback on the evidence (insufficient seeds/LR sweep) from feedback on the idea itself, which the reviewer finds plausible — a distinction Lesson 37 says defuses unnecessary friction
It is an example of vague, unactionable feedback since it doesn't request a specific fix
It should be read as a personal critique of the author's competence
questions.explain: Lesson 37 gives almost this exact sentence as its example of separating skepticism about evidence sufficiency from skepticism about the idea itself, and names this distinction as what defuses a lot of unnecessary friction in research feedback exchanges. It also names the seed count and LR-sweep question as concrete and actionable, not vague.

questions.code:
torch.onnx.export(
    model,
    example_input,  # batch size 1
    "model.onnx",
    input_names=["pixel_values"],
    output_names=["logits"],
    opset_version=17,
)
questions.prompt: This ONNX export omits the dynamic_axes argument, and the example input used during export has batch size 1. What happens in production, per Lesson 38?
options: The exported graph hardcodes the batch size from the example input, so the production system silently only accepts batch size 1
ONNX automatically infers flexible batch sizes for every export regardless of whether dynamic_axes is set
The export fails immediately with an error if dynamic_axes is omitted
Batch size has no effect on an ONNX export either way
questions.explain: Lesson 38 is explicit that dynamic_axes matters in practice: without it, the exported graph hardcodes the batch size from the example input used at export time, and the production system silently ends up with a model that only accepts that exact batch size — no error is raised, which makes this an easy mistake to miss until it causes a production issue.

questions.prompt: Select every piece of information Lesson 40 says must travel with a production model artifact so its lineage and quality are recoverable later.
options: The git commit hash at training time
The fully-resolved training config, not just the override flags someone typed
The exact version of the training dataset used
The name of the GPU model the training run happened to execute on
The eval harness that computed the metric the model was shipped on
questions.explain: Lesson 40 names three specific lineage pieces that must ship with a production artifact — commit hash, resolved config, and data version — and separately emphasizes that the eval harness itself must travel with the model as a regression test, not stay behind in the research repo. Which specific GPU model happened to run the training is not one of the required lineage pieces the lesson names.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 41 recommends the two-sample ________ test to compare a feature's distribution in recent production traffic against its distribution in the original training set, producing a p-value for whether the two are statistically distinguishable.
questions.explain: Lesson 41 uses scipy.stats.ks_2samp — the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test — as a concrete statistical check for data drift between a production window and the original training distribution.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order Lesson 39 describes for safely shipping a quantized model.
items: Train and finalize the model in the research repo as usual
Export the model with torch.quantization.quantize_dynamic to reduce its weights to int8
Re-run the original eval harness against the quantized artifact
Report the accuracy delta between the full-precision and quantized versions before shipping, not just the speedup
questions.explain: Lesson 39 is explicit that quantization has a real accuracy trade-off, and that you should always re-run the eval harness from the original research run against the quantized artifact before shipping, reporting the delta rather than only the speedup — this only makes sense in this order, after the model has already been trained and exported.

questions.prompt: A student is choosing a capstone paper. Paper A has no released code and must be reimplemented from the prose. Paper B requires multi-week, multi-hundred-GPU training exactly as the authors describe. Paper C has released code, runs on a single GPU in about a day, and has one clear headline accuracy number. Per Lesson 42, which paper should the student pick, and why?
options: Paper A, because reimplementing from prose builds deeper understanding
Paper B, because its scale makes the result more impressive to report
Paper C, because it passes all three filters: released code/checkpoints, modest compute, and one clear headline number — while A fails the first filter and B fails the second
Any of the three, since paper choice doesn't meaningfully affect whether a capstone succeeds
questions.explain: Lesson 42's three filters — released code and checkpoints, modest compute requirement, and one clear headline number — are applied in order, and a paper failing any one disqualifies it regardless of how interesting the result is. Paper A fails the code filter (reimplementing from prose is the backwards workflow Lesson 7 already warned against), Paper B fails the compute filter, and Paper C passes all three, making it the right choice. The lesson is explicit that most capstones fail because of the wrong paper choice, not because the student can't code.

questions.prompt: A capstone extension plan proposes removing the paper's regularizer, switching to a new dataset, and swapping the optimizer, all in the same experimental run, then attributing any change in the metric to 'the extension.' Select every true statement about this plan, per Lesson 44.
options: This combines more than one of the three extension shapes in a single run, which means the result can't attribute the effect to any one specific change
Lesson 44 recommends picking exactly one of the three extension shapes — ablation, new setting, or component swap — not combining them
This is a reasonable plan because combining changes always finds a bigger effect than testing them separately

If this combined extension shows no change in the metric at all, it isn't a clean, usable finding the way a well-scoped single-factor result would be, because the confound means you can't tell which change is responsible
questions.explain: Lesson 44 names ablation, new setting, and component swap as the three extension shapes and explicitly warns against combining more than one at once, since a capstone that ablates a component and changes the dataset and swaps the optimizer in the same run can't tell you which change caused what. A confounded result — positive, negative, or flat — can't be cleanly attributed, which is exactly why the lesson insists on isolating one factor at a time.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 45 calls an extension outcome with no measurable effect — reported with the same rigor as a positive finding — a ________ result.
questions.explain: Lesson 45 names the null result as a legitimate capstone outcome, reported with the same evidence (effect size, seed count, experiment design) as a positive finding, and explicitly says a clearly reasoned null result is a stronger outcome than an overstated positive one.
